1.pericope_label: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven: the title of the psalm and the four words for sin

schools.summary: Augustine grounds the deliverance in grace rather than the merits of works, and reads the absence of guile as the absence of boasted righteousness in a mouth whose conscience is full of sins.

Calvin takes the title from the whole scope of the psalm and makes the blessedness destroy the righteousness of works, refusing any half pardon; Gill reads forgiveness as a burden lifted off and carried away after the sin has been transferred to Christ the surety.

Henry prefers the reading that makes the title mean instruction and distinguishes no guile from no guilt; Spurgeon hears the psalm open with beatitudes and notes that the blessing falls on a forgiven lawbreaker, not a lawkeeper.

Clarke anatomises the four Hebrew words for evil and the three acts that remove them, and reports the headings the ancient versions gave the psalm; Wesley reduces the absence of guile to free confession and a whole-hearted turning.
Keil and Delitzsch pair the psalm with the one before it and place it as the second of the seven penitential psalms, composed after a year of condemnation following the adultery.

debates: What does the title Maschil mark? Henry allows it may be only a tune name but prefers the sense of instruction, Calvin denies that it is drawn from the promise to instruct later in the psalm and takes it from the whole scope, and Clarke calls it instructive by way of eminence and dates the psalm after the transgression with Bath-sheba.

What is it for a spirit to be without guile? Augustine takes it as having no boastings of righteousness in the mouth while the conscience is full of sins, Henry insists the text says no guile rather than no guilt and means sincerity rather than innocence, and Wesley makes it free confession and a turning from sin with the whole heart.
outliers: Clarke reports the headings the ancient versions gave the psalm: the Syriac makes it a psalm concerning the sin of Adam and a prophecy concerning Christ, the Arabic a prophecy of the redemption.
Calvin turns the verse into a polemic against the distinction between remitting the punishment and remitting the fault, which he calls only half a pardon.
themes: blessedness grounded in forgiveness rather than merit
the four words for sin and the three acts that remove it
sin lifted off and carried away
sincerity rather than innocence in the pardoned
pardon needed to the last step of life

3.pericope_label: When I kept silence: the torment of the unconfessed sin and the confession that ended it

schools.summary: Spurgeon renders the torment at full strength, comparing the inquest of conscience to the rack and the inquisition; Henry insists that repentance and confession do not merit pardon though they are needful to the enjoyment of it.

Gill reads the silence as senseless unconcern, takes the heavy hand as an unremitting affliction and perhaps a literal fever, and notes that the confession uses the same three words for sin as the doctrine of pardon above.
Clarke describes the horror before confession and then the sequence of things felt that ended in forgiveness; Wesley reads the failing spirit and decayed body as the effect of withheld confession.

Ellicott traces the ancient readings of the word for moisture to a misread letter, takes the drought figuratively of soul-fever rather than of a real fever, and rearranges the confession verse so that the words I said stand at its head.

debates: Is the drought of summer a real sickness or a figure? Gill thinks the heavy hand may design some violent distemper, perhaps a fever, and Ellicott answers that although some understand it literally it is better taken figuratively of the soul-fever which the whole passage describes.

Does the confession verse stand as it is? Ellicott alone will not read it as it stands, arguing from the future verbs that the words I said have changed their place and belong at the beginning, while Gill, Clarke, Henry and Wesley all expound the received order.
outliers: Ellicott assembles a chain of ancient readings for the word rendered moisture, fresh oil, an oily cake, the breast of oil, the thorn fixed in and spoiling in summer desolation, and traces them all to one misread letter taken for a preposition.

Spurgeon measures the pangs of conviction against the rack, the wheel and the flaming fagot, and says the Spanish inquisition with all its tortures was nothing to the inquest conscience holds within the heart.
themes: the torment of unconfessed sin
the heavy hand felt day and night
soul-fever rather than bodily fever
confession as wide as the pardon
pardon following immediately upon confession

6.pericope_label: For this shall every one that is godly pray: the time of finding, the floods, and the hiding place

schools.summary: Spurgeon makes the time of finding a term that expires once sentence has gone forth, and notes how one answered prayer quickens others; Henry grounds continued safety in God keeping his people from trouble by keeping them from sin, and will not let the songs of deliverance stay private.

Gill holds that all trespasses were forgiven at once by one eternal act for the sake of Christ, so the prayer must be for the manifestation of pardon to the conscience, and he limits the promise to preservation from being swallowed up by trouble rather than from having it.

Clarke locates the time of finding in the softened heart and alarmed conscience, and reads the hiding place as the city of refuge with the avenger of blood shut out; Wesley keeps both to the plain sense of a season of offered grace and a calamity that does not overwhelm.

Ellicott treats the phrase time of finding as an ellipsis better filled by a general word than by forgiveness, citing the ancient versions, and leaves the floods open between judgment and trial; Keil and Delitzsch turn the verse into a summons to every godly man who longs for mercy.

debates: When is the time in which God may be found? Clarke makes it the moment the heart is softened and the conscience alarmed, since God is ever ready and men are not; Spurgeon makes it a term that closes when sentence is pronounced; Wesley keeps it to the season of offered grace; and Ellicott declines to supply forgiveness at all, preferring a general word and citing the versions that render it the appointed time and opportune.

What do the godly ask for when they pray for pardon? Gill answers that no new act of pardon can arise in the mind of God or pass in the court of heaven, all trespasses having been forgiven at once for the sake of Christ, so that the prayer is for the manifestation of pardon to the conscience; Clarke, Wesley and Spurgeon treat the petition as a request for the thing itself in a time of finding.
outliers: Clarke identifies the hiding place with the city of refuge, so that the avenger of blood cannot overtake the man inside an impregnable wall.

Spurgeon accounts for the spread of prayer by a prospector image, that where one man finds a golden nugget others feel inclined to dig, and reckons that thousands have sought God with courage because of this one case.
themes: the time when God may be found
pardon prayed for and pardon manifested
floods that do not come nigh
the hiding place and the city of refuge
songs of deliverance shared in the congregation

8.pericope_label: I will instruct thee: the promise of guidance and the warning against the horse and the mule

schools.summary: Spurgeon takes the Lord as speaker and turns the guiding eye into a household discipline of whispers rather than thunderbolts, adding that pardon is given for education in holiness; Henry adds that God teaches by his word and guides by secret intimations of his will.

Gill reports the common view that the Lord is the speaker and lists the means of his instruction, and reads the horse and mule as three degrees of fault, unteachable, untractable, and hostile to those who teach.

Clarke takes the words as probably the Lord addressed to David and makes the guidance mutual, warning against forcing God to govern by affliction; Wesley has David bring God in as answering his prayers, and recalls the look given to Peter.

Keil and Delitzsch deny that God is the speaker and make the poet himself take up the teacher role; Ellicott prefers to hear words of deliverance sounding in the psalmist ears, and reports that the text of the following verse has suffered and its exact meaning is lost.

debates: Who speaks the promise of instruction? Spurgeon, Clarke, Wesley and Gill all take it as the Lord answering the prayer, while Keil and Delitzsch object that the addressee would then be a poet who already possesses the knowledge, and make him the teacher instead; Ellicott, with Ewald, Hitzig and Reuss, hears words of deliverance rather than a speaker at all.

Can the clause about the mouth held with bit and bridle be construed? Gill, Clarke and Wesley read it plainly as compulsion, and Wesley adds that all the ancient translators do the same, while Ellicott holds that the text has evidently suffered, the word rendered mouth meaning ornament elsewhere, and reports the Septuagint and Vulgate reading of jaws.
outliers: Spurgeon reckons those thrice happy who never sat at the feet of Gamaliel and know nothing of Aristotle or the ethics of the schools, yet have learned to follow the Lamb.
Wesley finds the promise to guide with the eye already fulfilled once in the look the Lord turned upon Peter.
themes: who speaks the promise of instruction
guidance by a look rather than a blow
pardon given for training in holiness
the horse and the mule as unreason
a text whose exact meaning is lost

10.pericope_label: Many sorrows shall be to the wicked: the two portions and the closing call to gladness

schools.summary: Spurgeon keeps the horse and mule in view for the wicked, contrasts a hive of wasps with a swarm of bees, and makes joy an act of obedience rather than a privilege.

Gill divides the sorrows into bodily ruin and awakened conscience, concedes the prosperity of the wicked while denying them peace in it, and follows the Targum in reading the gladness as gladness in Christ the essential Word.

Clarke binds sin to misery as firmly as holiness to happiness, roots happiness in holiness maintained by union with God, and suggests the last verse belongs to the next psalm; Wesley takes the sorrows as an argument enforcing the preceding admonition.
Keil and Delitzsch read the last verse as the deliberate close of the psalm, a short ending answering the short introduction after the doctrine has been unfolded in three unequal groups.

debates: Does the closing verse belong to this psalm at all? Clarke suggests it probably belongs to the psalm following and was originally its first verse, while Keil and Delitzsch make it the designed close, matching in brevity the introduction and rounding off three unequal groups of verses.

In what does the commanded gladness consist? Gill takes it, with the Targum, as gladness in the Word of the Lord and so in Christ and his imputed righteousness; Clarke roots it in a holiness kept up by continual union with God; Spurgeon makes it a matter of obedience, so that murmuring is rebellion.
outliers: Spurgeon contrasts the two portions as a hive of wasps around the wicked and a swarm of bees storing honey for those who trust.
Gill takes the Targum reading, gladness in the Word of the Lord, as evidence that the rejoicing is in Christ the essential Word and the righteousness imputed through him.
themes: the sorrows bound to wickedness
prosperity held with a curse
mercy surrounding the trusting
gladness commanded as obedience
the close of the psalm
